sections.h2: Who to call in Jacksonville and Duval County
sections.html:
Jacksonville and Duval County are consolidated, and two city departments split the property tax work. The Property Appraiser values parcels and decides exemptions. The Tax Collector sends the bills and takes the money. Both post their pages on jacksonville.gov.

The appraiser's Customer Service and Exemptions Division is at 231 E. Forsyth Street, Suite 260, phone 904-255-5900. The collector is on the same street at 231 E. Forsyth Street, main line (904) 255-5700. Its weekday counter opens at half past eight and closes at half past four. Value petitions go through the Value Adjustment Board at (904) 255-5124.

If downtown is a hassle, the collector also runs branches at Yates (main), Mandarin, Neptune Beach, North Main Street, Roosevelt, Soutel and Westside, plus a newer St Johns Square branch at 11160 Beach Blvd., Suite 121. That branch replaced the Kernan and Hogan offices, both permanently closed.

Every Duval parcel carries a district code, and the code decides which taxing authorities apply. There are six: GS and USD1 for Jacksonville, USD2 for Jacksonville Beach, USD3 for Atlantic Beach, USD4 for Neptune Beach and USD5 for Baldwin.

A district's total millage is built from separate levies. Countywide those are the county, the public schools, the Florida Inland Navigation District and the St. Johns River Water Management District. The three beach cities and the Town of Baldwin add their own municipal levies. Within one district, homes and businesses see the same millage unless a statute or local ordinance exempts something.

The appraiser posts a millage chart for each year back to 1999, which lets you see how your district's total has moved. The individual levies are set at public meetings in September, and the dates appear on the mailed notice.

Florida's yearly calendar repeats in Duval, so the same steps return every year.

Duval County property tax steps
StepWhen it happens
Preliminary tax roll approvedLate July
TRIM notices mailedAugust
Final tax roll certifiedOctober
Tax bills mailed by the collectorOn or about November 1
Timely homestead filing for the 2027 rollMarch 1, 2027
Tangible personal property returnApril 1 each year
Delinquency dateApril 1

If a mortgage servicer pays your tax from escrow, ask which bill it paid before you request a payoff, so nothing gets paid twice.

Owners who bought and moved in after January 1, 2026 can file online for the 2027 roll. A paper form can be mailed to Suite 260, faxed to (904) 255-7963 or emailed to the customer service address on the appraiser's page.

  • The home must be your permanent residence, or that of someone who depends on you, on January 1 of the roll year.
  • Some situations call for extra documents; the online form prompts for them at the end.
  • A previous Florida homestead may let you carry over part of the Save Our Homes difference through portability.

You can still file late until the 25th day after the August notices go out, which lands in early September. When you sell, your exemption stays behind. The buyer files fresh for the following roll.

Begin with an informal review at the appraiser's office. If that does not settle it, file a DR-486 petition with the Value Adjustment Board. The deadline is printed on your TRIM notice.

One practical detail: if you ask for the property record card with your petition, it is not mailed. You will find it online in Property Search, under the TRIM record card link just below the notice section. If the page will not open or print, call 904-255-5900.

The Board's page also cautions that petitioners generally must pay 75 percent of the ad valorem tax, plus every non-ad valorem charge, before the usual April 1 delinquency date, or the petition can be denied. Call the Board at (904) 255-5124 to learn your own figure.

The imagery on the appraiser's site does not always show true boundaries, and the office says it should not be relied on in a purchase. Use a surveyor and a title company for any sale.

The same page says Florida law requires the office to inspect every property in the county at least once every five years. Staff do not go inside homes. Appraisers drive marked vehicles, wear shirts with the city seal and carry City of Jacksonville identification, which helps if someone knocks and claims to be from the office.

Because the images are also used by Realtors and appraisers, a buyer may have studied your roofline before the first showing.

The Duval Clerk runs a free Property Fraud Alert. Sign up with a personal or business name, and an alert arrives within 48 hours after any document is recorded under that name in Duval County.

Scammers file bogus deeds to pose as owners, then rent or sell homes that are not theirs. Empty or inherited houses make easy targets, so a seller holding a vacant property gains the most from enrolling.

Report suspected exemption fraud to the appraiser's hotline at (904) 255-7964. If a family house is still in the name of someone who died, the unresolved ownership can affect the homestead. The appraiser's page points to Jacksonville Area Legal Aid and LISC Jacksonville for heirs' property help and says probate or another legal process may be needed.

Two obligations appear when a Duval home hosts short stays. Transient rentals owe additional sales and use tax to the Tax Collector every month, and furnishings in a rental count as taxable tangible personal property.

  • Airbnb, VRBO and similar sites do not send the tax to Duval for their users, so the owner remits it. Questions go to TouristTax@coj.net.
  • Household goods for your own use are excluded, but furniture and appliances in any rental, short or long, count.
  • Anyone owning such property on January 1 files a return by April 1.

Renting the home also ends the homestead, which raises taxable value after the next January 1.

Ask the collector for a payoff on every open year, confirm the parcel matches your deed and keep a copy of the closing statement. The state deed tax is seventy cents for every hundred dollars of price, and the recording clerk collects it.

Gather your photo ID, the deed, the latest tax bill and your mortgage statement before you meet the title agent. The agent orders the payoff, divides the year's tax between you and the buyer, and pays what you owe from your proceeds, so you do not need cash on hand. Look at the draft settlement statement a few days early and compare each tax line with the collector's figure.

Some owners hold separate benefits at the appraiser. A disabled former servicemember rated 10 percent or more gets $5,000 off assessed value. A deferral under Form DR-570 is filed with the collector by March 31. Ask whether a local older-owner exemption applies to your parcel. A cash buyer can usually close on a short schedule, which helps when a tax deadline is close.

faqs.q: Where is the Duval County tax collector's main office?
faqs.a: It is at 231 E. Forsyth Street, Jacksonville, FL 32202, phone (904) 255-5700, open Monday to Friday from half past eight until half past four. A newer branch operates at 11160 Beach Blvd., Suite 121.

faqs.q: When are TRIM notices mailed in Duval County?
faqs.a: In August each year. The petition deadline for the Value Adjustment Board is printed on each notice, so check your own.

faqs.q: Can I file for homestead online in Duval County?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners who moved into a Duval home after January 1, 2026 can use the online application for the 2027 roll. The timely deadline is March 1, 2027, and late filing runs to early September.

faqs.q: Does Airbnb collect Duval tourist tax for me?
faqs.a: No. Hosting sites do not remit tax directly to Duval County for users, so the property owner sends it to the Tax Collector's office.

faqs.q: How do I get notified if someone records a deed under my name?
faqs.a: Sign up for the Duval Clerk's free Property Fraud Alert at duvalclerk.gov. It watches a personal or business name and emails you within 48 hours of a matching recording.
